claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by electron–phonon coupling.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder modulates electron–phonon coupling.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder induces local lattice strain.
Local lattice strain alters superconducting pairing interactions.
The proposed initial material is a disordered, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy that is superconducting in an as-cast or rapidly cooled state.
Controlled thermal annealing can reduce chemical disorder without changing the alloy's overall composition.
The annealed and untreated samples should have identical overall compositions and similar grain structures so that chemical disorder is the principal controlled difference.
Local atomic-scale disorder produces spatial fluctuations in lattice strain.
Intrinsic chemical randomness in a high-entropy alloy enhances interband scattering.
Enhanced interband scattering modifies the electron–phonon interaction.
Reducing disorder by annealing decreases local lattice-strain variations.
Decreasing local lattice-strain variations strengthens electron–phonon coupling.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling promotes Cooper-pair formation and raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Annealed samples with less chemical disorder will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the untreated baseline.
Annealed samples will have a more spatially uniform superconducting gap than the untreated baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit less scattering-induced broadening than the untreated baseline.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate in near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys lacking significant magnetic impurities and secondary phases.
X-ray diffraction peak widths or transmission electron microscopy can be used to characterize the relevant change in chemical disorder.
Normal-state resistivity can serve as an indicator of scattering rate.

A lack of statistically significant improvement in transition temperature or gap uniformity after verified disorder reduction, or a lack of correlation with electron–phonon coupling parameters, would falsify the hypothesis.
